verdict.reasoning: Patient describes lip swelling after eating prawn soup: 'I ordered a prawn one this time... now I feel that there is a swelling. There is like a swelling on my upper lip.'

Onset and progression: 'That must have been... around seven.' and 'must have been like, I don't know, half an hour maybe' and 'there is like a swelling on my upper lip and it's kind of getting bigger... it feels like it's getting worse.'

Location and quality: 'my lips start feeling a little weird. Just in the, in the corner, sort of on the left first... now I feel that there is a swelling... on my upper lip' and 'you can still feel it, like really pumping blood.'
Breathing difficulty: Doctor asks about throat swelling; patient replies, 'Yeah, actually I feel like I can't breathe that well. Right now.'

Chest/breathing symptoms: Doctor asks, 'do you feel like your chest is tight?' Patient: 'I don't know. Chest just generally feels a little difficult... Yeah, it might be. I'm not sure.' This supports chest discomfort and difficult breathing, though 'tight' is uncertain but paraphrased.
Timing: 'That must have been just after work. So maybe like around seven.' and doctor repeats 'around seven o' clock.'

Prior similar episode: 'maybe I remember like a year ago... late night kind of Chinese place... after like having that very late, I woke up the next morning quite swollen up... Felt really bad and quite difficult breathing, but I don't know what it was. I had. It was like a curry or something.'
Asthma history: 'Well, I generally have asthma... I do take that regularly, but I've always taken it. I generally have asthma.'
Salbutamol use: 'I tell. I take. What's it called? Salbutamol inhalus... Yeah. So I do take that regularly.'
No other inhalers: Doctor asks, 'any other inhalers? Is it just the salbutamol that you use? Any other brown inhalers?' Patient: 'No, I don't think so.'

Peanut allergy and childhood severe reaction: 'So I have a peanut allergy as well... And any point... you had to ever use like an injection? Patient: 'When I was a kid, I think I remember my mom told me about it... Has your mom ever said that you had to go to hospital because you had a severe allergic reaction? Patient: 'Yeah, well, I was like six or something.' This supports prior hospital visit and injection in childhood.

Transcript shows her mother arrives later and is present ('Somebody just came... Mom, do we have any antihistamines around?'), but it does not state that the patient lives with or is currently staying with her mother; long-term living arrangement is not specified.

Doctor’s assessment: 'it sounds like you could be going into what we say, anaphylactic reaction' after prawn exposure with 'swelling of your lips,' 'I feel like I can't breathe that well,' chest feeling 'a little difficult,' history of peanut allergy, and a prior similar reaction with swelling and difficult breathing. This matches the composite description.
Asthma as active diagnosis: 'Well, I generally have asthma... I do take [salbutamol] regularly, but I've always taken it. I generally have asthma.' indicates current/ongoing asthma.

Emergency services: 'I think we need to call an ambulance... I'll call the ambulance. Okay. And I'll send them right to you.' and later instructing mom to 'call the 999... say that there is a suspected anaphylactic reaction and they need to come straight away.'
Interim antihistamine: 'Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around in the interim while we are waiting?' and 'So straight away, take the antihistamines in the meantime.'

Not alone and mother to call 999: Doctor asks if someone is with her, then says, 'Make sure that person's with you till the ambulance comes' and to mom: 'Mom, if you can call the 999... they need to come straight away.' This implies mother should stay with her and call 999.

Post-ED follow-up for injections: 'Come out from the hospital. Do give us a ring back. We might need to sort you out with your injections and things like that.' which refers to arranging allergy injections (e.g., autoinjector) and further management after emergency care.
